You are a literature-research subagent. Do NOT write any files. Return findings as your final text reply only. Use WebSearch and WebFetch (load them via ToolSearch "select:WebSearch,WebFetch" first). Work autonomously; no human will answer questions. Use American spelling.

TASK: Collect QUANTITATIVE validation statistics of heliospheric solar-wind models at 1 AU (ambient/background solar wind, not just CMEs). For each number give: paper (authors, year, journal), the table/figure/section it comes from, and a URL or DOI. Clearly flag any number you could not verify from source text (do not quote numbers from memory without saying so). Prefer open-access full text (arXiv, AGU Space Weather open access, Frontiers, Solar Physics open access, A&A open access) so you can read the actual tables.

Papers to cover (find more if relevant):
- Jian, MacNeice, Taktakishvili et al. 2015 Space Weather "Validation for solar wind prediction at Earth: Comparison of coronal and heliospheric models installed at the CCMC" (speed/density/B correlation, RMSE, skill; HSS/SIR event-based metrics; does WSA-ENLIL under- or over-predict density and B?).
- Jian et al. 2016 (Space Weather or ApJ) validation for SIRs/CIRs at STEREO.
- Owens et al. 2008 Space Weather (WSA-ENLIL, CCMC, speed and B errors, time-shift).
- Reiss et al. 2016 Space Weather (ESWF empirical solar wind forecast; RMSE of speed), Reiss et al. 2019 ApJS "Forecasting the ambient solar wind with numerical models. I. On the implementation of an operational framework" (WSA/PFSS/HUX: RMSE, MAE, correlation, event-based skill), Reiss et al. 2020 Space Weather (ensemble), Reiss et al. 2023 Space Weather "Unifying the validation of ambient solar wind models" (ISWAT team).
- Hinterreiter et al. 2019 Solar Physics "Assessing the performance of EUHFORIA modeling the background solar wind" (RMSE, MAE, ME of speed; HSS hits/misses/false alarms; timing errors).
- Riley et al. (e.g., Riley, Linker, Mikic 2013 / Riley et al. 2015 "Predicting the solar wind" MAS-CORHEL statistics), MacNeice 2009 WSA validation.
- Owens et al. 2020 Solar Physics HUXt (benchmark vs HelioMAS; speed errors).
- Lang & Owens 2019 Space Weather (BRaVDA variational data assimilation) and Lang et al. 2021 Space Weather "Improving solar wind forecasting using data assimilation": RMSE reduction from data assimilation; Lang & Owens 2021?
- Samara et al. 2021/2022 (EUHFORIA dynamic time warping), Baker et al., Milosic et al. 2023 EUHFORIA validation, Kay?, Hinterreiter.
- Also any statements on ENLIL density underprediction/overprediction at 1 AU, magnetic field underprediction ("open flux problem", B underpredicted by factor ~2), and timing errors of HSS arrival (e.g., ±1 day).

Return a compact but complete markdown report (can be long, up to ~1500 words) with a table of: model, paper, period, speed RMSE (km/s), speed correlation r, density metrics (bias, r), B metrics, event-based HSS metrics (hits/misses/false alarms, timing error), DA skill gain. Include URLs/DOIs for each. End with the key one-paragraph synthesis. Flag unverified numbers explicitly.

<system-reminder>
Your final report is delivered through SubagentHandback: when your work is complete, call SubagentHandback({message: <your full report>}). The call ends your run, so make it your last step. Only a SubagentHandback call reaches your caller as your result; plain text you write at the end is not delivered. Do not also send the report with SendMessage: your caller would get it twice.
</system-reminder>

The paper you're asking about is Jian et al. (2015), published in *Space Weather* volume 13, issue 5, pages 316–338. The search turned up its abstract and bibliographic details.

- **Scope:** The authors ran four CCMC-hosted models (WSA-Enlil, MAS-Enlil, SWMF, and IPS-based heliospheric tomography) in 10 combinations. They tested them against OMNI near-Earth data for seven Carrington rotations in 2007, during the late declining phase of solar cycle 23 ([index 2-1, 2-2, 2-3](https://deepblue.lib.umich.edu/items/0e5aba2b-1fb1-4f29-af41-6deae8aa233c)).
- **Main findings:** MAS-Enlil best reproduced the time patterns of solar wind parameters, while WSA-Enlil tracked normalized parameters more closely. The authors also found that visual comparison is needed alongside quantitative metrics ([index 2-4, 2-5](https://deepblue.lib.umich.edu/items/0e5aba2b-1fb1-4f29-af41-6deae8aa233c)).
- **Structures:** For sector boundaries, the new MAS-Enlil version performed best. For slow-to-fast stream interaction regions, heliospheric tomography did best. The new SWMF version needed more development ([index 2-9, 2-10](https://deepblue.lib.umich.edu/items/0e5aba2b-1fb1-4f29-af41-6deae8aa233c)).
- **Bibliographic note:** A CU Experts record lists 94 citations for this paper ([index 3-1](https://vivo.colorado.edu/display/pubid_312121)). The authors later published a follow-up on Ulysses comparisons in *Space Weather* 14(8), 2016 ([index 7-1](https://vivo-cub.colorado.edu/display/pubid_312143)).

I only had the abstract and metadata, not the full text, so the details of the methods and metrics are not verified beyond these summaries.

The paper is Reiss et al. (2019), "Forecasting the Ambient Solar Wind with Numerical Models. I. On the Implementation of an Operational Framework," published in ApJS 240, 35. Its arXiv ID is 1905.04353, submitted 10 May 2019.

- **Scope:** The authors build an operational framework around Carrington Rotation 2077. They use the PFSS and Schatten current sheet models for the coronal field, and compare the Wang–Sheeley, distance-from-coronal-hole-boundary, and WSA relations for solar wind conditions near the Sun. Carrington Rotation 2077 is the test case, with the coronal magnetic field reconstructed by the PFSS and SCS models and three empirical relations compared (WS, DCHB, and WSA).
- **Ensemble and HUX:** They vary the sub-Earth latitude to build an ensemble of initial conditions, then map results to Earth with the HUX model (ensemble members are mapped to Earth through the Heliospheric Upwind eXtrapolation model).
- **Main result:** WSA gave the lowest speed error, with an RMSE of about 83 km/s, and ensembling modestly improved all models (WSA most accurately predicts the speed time series, and ensemble forecasting slightly improves every model tested).

Sources: the arXiv PDF (arxiv.org/abs/1905.04353), the IOP/ApJS article (doi 10.3847/1538-4365/aaf8b3), and the ar5iv HTML render. The arXiv abstract page lists the submission date and authors. Part II (arXiv 2003.09336) is a separate follow-up paper on an adaptive prediction system.

Links: [{"title":"Implementing the MULTI-VP coronal model in EUHFORIA: test case results and comparisons with the WSA coronal model","url":"https://arxiv.org/pdf/2102.06617"},{"title":"arxiv.org","url":"https://arxiv.org/abs/1907.07461v2"},{"title":"scholars.unh.edu","url":"https://scholars.unh.edu/cmerg/394"},{"title":"pp521 Hinterreiter Assessing%20the%20performance%20of%20EUHFORIA%20modeling%20the%20background%20solar%20wind reprint","url":"https://lirias.kuleuven.be/bitstream/123456789/645257/2/pp521-Hinterreiter-Assessing%20the%20performance%20of%20EUHFORIA%20modeling%20the%20background%20solar%20wind-reprint.pdf"},{"title":"publi2-as.oma.be","url":"https://publi2-as.oma.be/record/4092"},{"title":"research.fi","url":"https://research.fi/en/results/publication/0365650619"},{"title":"pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov","url":"https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6900206"},{"title":"zh.mindat.org","url":"https://zh.mindat.org/reference.php?id=8925396"},{"title":"Free Access","url":"https://www.aanda.org/articles/aa/full_html/2021/04/aa39325-20/aa39325-20.html"},{"title":"11institutetext: 1. SIDC, Royal Observatory of Belgium, Brussels, Belgium","url":"https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2102.06617"}]

The paper is on arXiv as **arXiv:1907.07461**, titled "Testing the background solar wind modelled by EUHFORIA." Its journal version is Hinterreiter et al. (2019), "Assessing the Performance of EUHFORIA Modeling the Background Solar Wind," in *Solar Physics* 294:170, DOI 10.1007/s11207-019-1558-8.

- **Method:** The authors ran the basic EUHFORIA 1.0.4 setup with default inputs, modeled background solar wind with no CMEs, and compared it against ACE in-situ data (modeled background solar wind (no coronal mass ejections) and compared the obtained results with ACE, in situ measurements). They built continuous time series from daily runs for statistical work.
- **Study periods:** Low-activity (2008) and high-activity (2012) intervals were examined. The low-activity phase matched observations better (a better match between model results and observations).
- **Findings:** Model quality varied. The authors also looked at coronal hole characteristics as sources of the fast streams and suggested ways to improve the model.
- **Later citations:** Later EUHFORIA work cites this paper for the finding that the velocities of slow and fast solar wind are frequently underestimated.

Sources: arXiv abstract page (https://arxiv.org/abs/1907.07461v2), the Solar Physics reprint (PMC6900206 and the KU Leuven PDF), and the UNH scholars record.

L. K. Jian1,2, P. J. MacNeice2, A. Taktakishvili2,3, D. Odstrcil2,4, B. Jackson5, H.-S. Yu5, P. Riley6,

1Department of Astronomy, University of Maryland, College Park, Maryland, USA, 2Heliophysics Science Division, NASA

Washington, District of Columbia, USA, 4School of Physics, Astronomy, and Computational Sciences, George Mason

Abstract Multiple coronal and heliospheric models have been recently upgraded at the Community
Coordinated Modeling Center (CCMC), including the Wang-Sheeley-Arge (WSA)-Enlil model, MHD-Around-a-Sphere
(MAS)-Enlil model, Space Weather Modeling Framework (SWMF), and heliospheric tomography using interplanetary
scintillation data. To investigate the effects of photospheric magnetograms from different sources, different
coronal models, and different model versions on the model performance, we run these models in 10 combinations.
Choosing seven Carrington rotations in 2007 as the time window, we compare the modeling results with the
Operating Mission as Nodes on the Internet data for near-Earth space environment during the late declining
phase of solar cycle 23. Visual comparison is proved to be a necessary addition to the quantitative assessment of
the models’ capabilities in reproducing the time series and statistics of solar wind parameters. The MAS-Enlil
model captures the time patterns of solar wind parameters better, while the WSA-Enlil model matches with the
time series of normalized solar wind parameters better. Models generally overestimate slow wind temperature
and underestimate fast wind temperature and magnetic ﬁeld. Using improved algorithms, we have identiﬁed
magnetic ﬁeld sector boundaries (SBs) and slow-to-fast stream interaction regions (SIRs) as focused structures.
The success rate of capturing them and the time offset vary largely with models. For this quiet period, the new
version of MAS-Enlil model works best for SBs, while heliospheric tomography works best for SIRs. The new
version of SWMF with more physics added needs more development. General strengths and weaknesses for
each model are diagnosed to provide an unbiased reference to model developers and users.
1. Motivation
We are motivated to validate the coronal and heliospheric models for the quasi-steady solar wind from the
following three respects. First, a stream interaction region (SIR) forms when fast wind overtakes and interacts
with the proceeding slow wind. It is in nature the same as the commonly known corotating interaction
region [e.g., Smith and Wolfe, 1976; Gosling and Pizzo, 1999]. However, we use SIRs to emphasize that when
the solar background changes within one Carrington rotation (CR), the resultant SIRs are short lived and do
not corotate with the Sun to recur. In fact, Jian et al. [2006, 2011a] ﬁnd 51% of SIRs near solar maximum and
10% at solar minimum do not recur at Earth. Large-amplitude Alfvén waves [Belcher and Davis, 1971] in SIRs
and the following fast wind can drive a series of particle injections and affect the evolution of outer radiation
belt (centered at about 4 RE), as demonstrated in Miyoshi and Kataoka [2005]. Additionally, in geomagnetic

8. Validation for Slow-to-Fast Stream Interactions
Because solar wind speed is a robust parameter every model can provide and it has the best observational
coverage, we use it to identify the SIRs. The algorithm for automatic detection is revised based on Owens
et al. [2005] and MacNeice [2009a], and it includes 10 steps. We have applied the algorithm to observations
and each model result to assure major SIRs are successfully captured. (1) Mark all time points which are
more than 50 km/s faster than 1 day earlier. (2) Eliminate any isolated single data points which are marked.
(3) Group each contiguous block of marked points as a distinct high speed enhancement (HSE) and ﬁnd
the start and end time of each HSE. (4) For each HSE, ﬁnd the minimum speed starting 2 days ahead of the
HSE till the start of the HSE, and mark it as the minimum speed (Vmin) of the HSE; ﬁnd the maximum
speed starting from the beginning of the HSE through 1 day after the HSE and mark it as the maximum
speed (Vmax) of the HSE. (5) For each HSE, ﬁnd the last time reaching Vmin and the ﬁrst time reaching Vmax
and mark them as the start and end time of an SIR. (6) Combine SIRs separated by less than 0.75 day and
eliminate any repeated count of SIRs. (7) Reject any SIRs shorter than 0.5 day. (8) For the regrouped SIRs,
ﬁnd the Vmin and Vmax for each SIR and mark the last time of highest speed gradient as the stream
interface (SI), the boundary between slow and fast wind. Eliminate SIRs with the redundant SI time. (9)
Reject any SIRs with Vmin faster than 500 km/s, or Vmax slower than 400 km, or speed increase less than
100 km/s. (10) Reject SIRs crossing two CRs because the simulation results are choppy crossing two CRs
even after smoothing.
